title: Japan’s first fall color forecast for 2026 is here!
description: Maps and predicated peak color dates to help you plan your autumn journey to see Japan’s natural beauty. There are a lot of reasons why fall is a great time of year to travel in Japan, such as sunny weather, not-too-hot, not-too-cold temperatures, and smaller crowds. The absolute best reason for an autumn trip, though, […]
content:
Maps and predicated peak color dates to help you plan your autumn journey to see Japan’s natural beauty.

There are a lot of reasons why fall is a great time of year to travel in Japan, such as sunny weather, not-too-hot, not-too-cold temperatures, and smaller crowds. The absolute best reason for an autumn trip, though, is to see the beautiful fall colors.

In particular, Japan’s maple and ginkgo trees, or kaede and icho if you’re using their Japanese names, are what turn many of the country’s forests, gardens, and temples into a patchwork of vivid reds and yellows every autumn. Of course, there’s a timing element involved in seeing fall foliage. Head out to see it too early, and the leaves will still be in their summer-green state, but go too late, and you run the risk of the leaves being brown and withered, or maybe even having fallen off, leaving you looking at bunches of barren branches.

So to help travelers coordinate their travel plans with Mother Nature’s, Japan Meteorological Corporation has prepared a fall foliage forecast. Generally speaking, the fall colors sweep across Japan in the opposite direction that the cherry blossoms do, starting in the north, where cooler weather sets in earlier, and then moving down to east Japan, followed by the western part of the country. There’s an additional wrinkle, though, in that high-altitude areas, typically further inland from the coastline, also tend to see their leaves change color earlier than lower-lying areas.

First, let’s take a look at the forecast maps showing when the leaves are predicted to be at their most breathtakingly bright shades of red and yellow.

▼ Peak maple color forecast map showing Sapporo (札幌), Sendai (仙台), Tokyo (東京), Nagoya (名古屋), Osaka (大阪), and Fukuoka (福岡)

▼ Peak ginkgo color forecast, also with Sapporo (札幌), Sendai (仙台), Tokyo (東京), Nagoya (名古屋), Osaka (大阪), and Fukuoka (福岡)

Compared to an average year, JMC is predicting that east Japan will turn crimson later than usual, and northern Japan’s yellow leaves will be arriving later as well. In addition to the above maps, they’ve also put together a list of the peak color dates by city.

● Predicted peak color for maple/ginkgo trees
Sapporo: November 7/November 6
Aomori: November 13/November 6
Sendai: November 25/November 29
Tokyo: November 29//November 26
Kanazawa: November 30/November 10
Nagano: November 20//November 14
Nagoya: December 2//November 17
Kyoto: December 11/November 27
Osaka: December 4/November 24
Wakayama: December 11/November 26
Hiroshima: November 28//November 20
Kochi: December 9/November 16
Fukuoka: December 7/November 27
Kagoshima: December 10/November 27

As we can see from the predicted dates, gingko trees usually reach their peak color before maples, so does this mean you’ll have to pick between seeing one or the other? Not necessarily. Unlike the cherry blossoms, which appear for only a bittersweetly short time, the fall colors can be enjoyed for a longer period. Sure, it can be tricky to time a trip to see both the maples and gingko at their absolute prettiest condition at the same place at the same time, but there’s enough overlap so that if one of the leaf types is looking its best, the other is probably very photogenic too. JMC is predicting this year’s overall fall color season to be:

● North Japan
Maple: Early October to mid-November in mountains, mid-October to late November in flatlands
Ginkgo: Early November to late November in flatlands
● East Japan
Maple: Late October to early December in mountains, late November to mid-December in flatlands
Ginkgo: Early November to early December in flatlands
● West Japan
Maple: Late October to early December in mountains, late November to mid-December in flatlands
Ginkgo: Mid-November to early December in flatlands

As we’re still at least a month away from the first signs of fall color, JMC will be updating its predictions as we get deeper into fall, but for now the forecast is enough to start forming plans from. And if you just can’t wait that long for your fall trip, Japan Railways has a new unlimited-ride train pass that can be activated from early October.

Source: Japan Meteorological Corporation, PR Times

title: Starbucks Japan reveals new Tsukimi Moon-Viewing drinkware and gifts for autumn 2026
description: New “Bunny Autumn Festival” collection celebrates the rabbit in the moon with sweet design details.  As we enter September, people across the nation are beginning to take notice of the encroaching night sky and the beauty of the moon, which appears particularly bright at this time of year. The moon-gazing culminates in Tsukimi (literally “moon-viewing“), […]
content:
New “Bunny Autumn Festival” collection celebrates the rabbit in the moon with sweet design details. 

As we enter September, people across the nation are beginning to take notice of the encroaching night sky and the beauty of the moon, which appears particularly bright at this time of year. The moon-gazing culminates in Tsukimi (literally “moon-viewing“), a cultural event that occurs around the time of the autumn full moon – this year the date is 25 September – and over at Starbucks, the celebrations have begun with a brand new Tsukimi collection.

Called “Bunny Autumn Festival“, the range taps into another celestial-related belief – that the markings on the moon look like a rabbit pounding rice. If you’ve ever held that image in your mind while gazing at the moon in Japan, you’ll see how the markings really do look more like a rabbit as opposed to a “man on the moon”, and it’s a beautiful way for companies like Starbucks to give moon-viewing goods an extra dash of cuteness.

The new range centres around the idea of a family of rabbits joyously celebrating the harvest festival, playing with mooncakes on a moonlit night. Though mooncakes aren’t commonly eaten here as they are in other parts of Asia, they add colour and cuteness to the collection while celebrating the moon that shines down on us all.

▼ The collection begins with the Stainless Steel To-Go Bottle, Rabbit Ivory – 473 millilitres (16 ounces) – 5,350 yen (US$33.42)

Shaped like a giant Starbucks cup, this stainless steel bottle features a locking lid for leak-proof peace-of-mind. The lid opens easily by pressing the button down and sliding it to the right.

The double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless steel construction provides excellent heat and cold retention, while the bunnies on the front provide excellent cuteness.

▼ Stainless Steel Tumbler with Replacement Lid, MiiR Rabbit Navy, 473 millilitres – 5,900 yen

The deep navy colour, reminiscent of the night sky, serves to highlight the rabbits, which can be seen leaping playfully across the bottom of the tumbler.

This item also boasts double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless steel construction, and is produced in collaboration with MiiR, a premium Seattle-based drinkware brand.

▼ Cold Cup Tumbler – 710 millilitres 3,050 yen

This product brings an air of sophistication to the range, with a starry, textured surface that catches the light, creating a beautiful, sparkly shine.

▼ The large 710-millilitre size allows you to enjoy more of your favourite beverage for longer.

▼ Cold Cup Tumbler, Rabbit Navy – 710 millilitres 2,700 yen

▼ This beautiful design features a full moon, with rabbits racing around it, against a dark night sky.

The removable lid makes this one particularly easy to clean, and like the three other items above, it comes with a free drink ticket.

▼ Stainless Steel Mug, Rabbit Coral Pink – 473 millilitres 4,200 yen

Those who prefer to drink Starbucks from a mug will be able to opt for this stylish stainless steel design, which features a wonderfully serene moment, with three bunnies gathered together under a golden moon.

▼ Double-walled vacuum insulation, and a removable lid to keep your drink hot, or cold, for longer.

Rounding out the collection are a couple of bear-y cute gifts, featuring the chain’s Bearista character.

▼ Bearista Message Gift (with drink ticket) 1,650 yen

▼ For this outing, the Bearista is dressed up in an adorable bunny costume.

The Bearista has magnets concealed in both hands, which allows it to hold the message card drink ticket firmly in place for premium presentation.

▼ It also has a loop between its ears so you can attach a keychain and use it as a charm.

The drink ticket itself is also beautifully designed, with golden embossed print and three cute rabbits under the green mermaid, surrounded by stars like a Starbucks moon.

▼ Completing the set is a gift bag so cute you’ll want to gift it to yourself.

▼ Beverage Card (with drink ticket) 750 yen

Shout someone a drink with the assistance of the sweet rabbit family, appearing on a coral-pink card that captures the fun and cosiness of moon-viewing season.

With so many different products at different price points, you don’t have to spend a lot to join the fun of moon-viewing at Starbucks this year. You’ll have to act like a bunny and jump quick, though, as the range became available online on 1 September, and at Starbucks stores on 2 September, and is only available in limited numbers while stocks last.

title: Elderly couple donates 400 million yen to erect Myaku-Myaku statue in Osaka
description: Multi-million-dollar Myaku-Myaku donation. It’s been nearly a year since the closing of the 2025 World Expo in Osaka, but its official mascot, the gooey humanoid Myaku-Myaku has managed to secure a popularity that has transcended the event it was created to represent. Myaku-Myaku goods are still widely sold, and game centers are still well stocked […]
content:
Multi-million-dollar Myaku-Myaku donation.

It’s been nearly a year since the closing of the 2025 World Expo in Osaka, but its official mascot, the gooey humanoid Myaku-Myaku has managed to secure a popularity that has transcended the event it was created to represent. Myaku-Myaku goods are still widely sold, and game centers are still well stocked with crane games offering chances at plush toys and other goods bearing its moist likeness.

It’s a rather surprising turn of events for the mascot after its debut in 2022, which left people unsure of how to feel about its characteristics, both cute, such as its big smile and stubby little legs, and grotesque, such as its head looking like bloody entrails.

▼ Early Myaku-Myaku fan art.

シニゲーくん pic.twitter.com/kiBndmNDva

— 色紙の妖精しきっしー (@SIKISSYfacerock) April 26, 2022

But over the years, people by and large seemed to really warm up to Myaku-Myaku. Its post-Expo activities have only continued to grow into projects such as a tastefully erotic photo book.

And now, a surprise donation to the City of Osaka may very well cement the mascot’s legacy for generations to come. Reports have recently come in that business owner Keihachi Fukunishi and his wife Akiyo Fukunishi, both 85, have given 200 million yen each, for a total of 400 million (US$2.5 million) yen to the city.

▼ There were already several statues at the venue, but the materials weren’t intended for permanent use.

The couple’s donation came with a request that a statue of Myaku-Myaku be erected on the site where the Expo was held. At a press event where Keihachi and Akiyo received letters of appreciation, the husband told reporters the Myaku-Myaku “is a symbol. Just as the Tower of the Sun defined the Senri Expo Park, Myaku-Myaku defines the Osaka-Kansai Expo.”

He makes an interesting comparison too. The Tower of the Sun was the centerpiece of the 1970 Expo, which was also held in Osaka and also wasn’t without controversy when first unveiled. Its creator, Taro Okamoto, created it in almost direct opposition to the post-moon-landing Expo’s overarching theme of technological progress by filling his statue with organic and tribalistic imagery.

▼ The Tower of the Sun

However, by the end of that Expo, it was widely lauded as a masterpiece and still stands today, designated as a national tangible cultural property. Perhaps Myaku-Myaku’s own shockingly organic appearance and subsequent rise to prominence reminded the Fukunishis of the Tower of the Sun, and they wanted to entrench the mascot’s legacy in the same way.

In response, Osaka mayor Hideyuki Yokoyama said, “I would like to accelerate deliberation so that Myaku-Myaku can take its place alongside the Grand Ring as a new symbol of this site.”

Another of the Expo’s highlights was the massive wooden Grand Ring that encompassed much of the venue and measured about two kilometers (1.2 miles) in circumference. All but a 200-meter stretch of it has been slated for demolition to make room for Japan’s first integrated resort and casino, which will be built next to a commemorative park that honors the Expo.

However, many readers of the news online were irked by Yokoyama’s promise to “accelerate deliberation” (kento wo kasoku), a typical non-committal phrase used by politicians to essentially say, “We’ll think about whether we want to do this or not as soon as we can.” On the other hand, some wonder if building a giant Myaku-Myaku statue might end up costing the people of Osaka in the long run.

“So, will they give the money back if they decide not to do it after their accelerated deliberations?”
“What is this accelerated deliberation nonsense? Just get it going so it’s built in time for that elderly couple to see it!”
“I hate hearing ‘accelerate deliberation,’ because it means it’ll probably never happen.”
“They’d do a lot more good by donating that money to fix the many deteriorating drainage pumps in the southern part of the city.”
“I wonder if the donors thought about maintenance costs. Seems a bit arrogant to me.”
“If they love Myaku-Myaku so much, why not build the statue in their own home?”
“Asking for a Myaku-Myaku statue just because you donate money gives me the same unsettling vibes as a corporation donating money for certain favors.”
“That’s a wonderful idea. They probably decided to donate the money while they’re still alive rather than just have it taken in inheritance taxes.”

The theory in that last comment seems very plausible. Given the age of the donors, it is entirely possible that they have no one who they need to leave the money to. Even if they do have heirs, a large chunk gets taken out in taxes, so why not pre-empt that along with a request as to how they’d like to see it spent?

They didn’t even say all the money needed to go into the statue, just that they’d like that to be done as a part of the donation. That being said, the idea of a giant Statue-of-Liberty-style Myaku-Myaku in the harbor of Osaka, defining the city’s skyline and welcoming everyone arriving by air and sea, is very appealing to me, and I’m not even that big a fan of the character.

Source: ABC News, Hachima Kiko

title: Japan’s revolving sushi restaurant king Sushiro coming to U.S. this fall with high prices, no tipping
description: Sushiro, budget-friendly in Japan, is adding private rooms and full-course meals as it arrives in America for the first time. Among Japan’s major kaiten/revolving sushi restaurant chains, Sushiro has the most passionate fans. Pretty much wherever a new Sushiro branch opens, you can expect crowds of sushi lovers looking to grab a seat at peak […]
content:
Sushiro, budget-friendly in Japan, is adding private rooms and full-course meals as it arrives in America for the first time.

Among Japan’s major kaiten/revolving sushi restaurant chains, Sushiro has the most passionate fans. Pretty much wherever a new Sushiro branch opens, you can expect crowds of sushi lovers looking to grab a seat at peak dining times, and this fall, for the first time, that’s probably going to be happening in America too.

Sushiro is just a few weeks away from opening its first-ever U.S. branch, and it’s not timidly testing the waters with a low-key launch in a low-competition market. Instead, it’s starting its American endeavor in New York’s Times Square.

▼ Though it was probably based more on real estate availability than issuing a direct challenge, America’s first Sushiro is located right next door to a McDonald’s.

Sushiro is leaning into its legacy of success in promoting the new restaurant, billing itself in English as the “world’s #1 sushi brand.” And yes, in some ways the preview images look similar to Sushiro branches in Japan, with large monitors near the entrance displaying the call numbers of parties whose tables are ready, and horizontally oriented touch panels with images of sushi digitally flowing by which can be tapped on to place orders.

However, there are a number of ways in which dining at Sushiro in the U.S. is going to be very different from eating at the chain’s restaurants in Japan. For one thing, Sushiro America appears to be trying to position itself as a much more premium dining destination. A two-piece plate of maguro (tuna) sushi, for example, will cost you 180 yen at Sushiro in Tokyo. In New York, though, a plate of maguro will cost US$5, equivalent to roughly 800 yen.

Granted, restaurant prices are higher in general in America than they are in Japan, and the current exchange rate makes the gap feel even bigger. That said, assuming a person were to eat five plates of maguro, that 900 yen would still be considered a rather modestly priced restaurant meal in Japan, whereas a $25 meal in the U.S., while not a major luxury in today’s economy, isn’t a particularly thrifty meal either. There’s also the fact that the New York Sushiro’s maguro will actually be cheaper than its other types of sushi, which will be priced at 6, 8, or 10 dollars a plate.

Further signs of Sushiro’s upscale American dream can be found in the New York branch’s private rooms, something not seen in chain revolving sushi restaurants in Japan. Located on a separate level of the restaurant from the other diners, each room has swanky minimalist décor and its own refined name, such as “Sho Chiku Bai,” “Wabi Sabi,” or “Yama Kawa Umi.”

If you’re wondering where the lanes that whisk your food to you are hidden in these private rooms, there aren’t any. Sushro says that these rooms provide patrons with “a Japanese private dining experience featuring a curated prix fixe course menu.”

That doesn’t mean no care will be given to the main dining area’s automatically delivered dishes, though, and Sushiro boasts that customers will be able to choose from some 200 menu items. Some of these will be original creations crafted specifically to cater to American tastes, such as a double-cheeese shrimp roll and marinated salmon with cream cheese.

▼ It’s also kind of unusual that Sushiro America is trying to make “Eat ‘til you drop” its catchphrase. Not only is the chain not known for large portions, the Japanese phrase kuidaore, which literally means “eat until you drop,” is already associated with the city of Osaka and its food culture as a whole, not just Sushiro’s Osaka-based parent company.

But while the Sushiro experience in America is going to have some differences from the one in the chain’s home country, there is one surprising way it’s going to be just like in Japan. The management has put the word out that the New York Sushiro will have a no-tipping policy, with the announcement being greeted with a round of applause by attendees at a preview event, reflecting a growing sense of fatigue among American consumers towards gratuities.

Sushiro’s New York branch is slated to open sometime this coming October.

Source: Nitele News via Hachima Kiko, Jiji, FNN Prime Online, Sushiro USA

title: The mystery of Port Store, the Japanese convenience store that looks like a Lawson rip-off
description: What looks like an anime convenience store is actually a heartwarming way to serve the local community. All the big-name convenience stores in Japan have instantly recognisable features that can easily be identified from a distance, and for Lawson, that means blue, white and pink stripes, and a distinctive milk can logo. Well, we thought […]
content:
What looks like an anime convenience store is actually a heartwarming way to serve the local community.


All the big-name convenience stores in Japan have instantly recognisable features that can easily be identified from a distance, and for Lawson, that means blue, white and pink stripes, and a distinctive milk can logo.

Well, we thought that was the case until our reporter Mr Sato stumbled upon this store in Aomi, just a stone’s throw from Tokyo’s famous Odaiba district.

▼ From a distance, this looks like a regular Lawson.

▼ But as you get closer…

▼ … you realise it’s something different.

The store looks identical to a Lawson – so much so that if you’re not paying attention you might even walk through its doors thinking as such, but look closely and you’ll see the words “Port Store” on the sign instead of Lawson.

▼ Even the milk can logo has “Port Store” branding.

A sight like this is enough to make you think you’ve stepped out of reality and into a parallel universe, because convenience stores are notoriously protective of their trademarks, and would never let a store like this rip off their branding in the real world.

▼ Yet here it is, existing like something out of an anime or video game, with everything telling you it’s a Lawson, except for the name.

Sensing he may have found a glitch in the system, Mr Sato walked towards the Port Store and stepped through its automatic doors.

Looking around, his brain short-circuited again, as he saw that the selections on offer were more or less the same as what you’d find at a regular Lawson. However, there were some products that appeared to be unique to this location, including work gloves, socks and towels, and work shoes and helmets.

Stopping for a moment, Mr Sato whipped out his phone and ran a search online to find out exactly what he had walked into, and that’s when he learned that the store is operated by the Tokyo Port Welfare Association in partnership with Lawson. The association is a non-profit that runs shops and other services for people working in Tokyo’s port areas, and by partnering with convenience stores like Lawson and Family Mart it was able to expand, providing port workers with easier access to essential work gear and leading to the “Port Store” branded convenience stores seen in some port areas today.

Being able to buy items normally sold at workwear stores is convenient for people who work in these areas, especially when these stores are open 24 hours. For Mr Sato, though, the store had three things that lured him into opening his wallet – a waffle cone milk ice cream, cheap cheese crackers, and a Toraichi towel.

Toraichi is a Japanese workwear brand, particularly well known among manual labourers, and something you normally wouldn’t find at a convenience store.

▼ Mr Sato, looking and feeling cool with his ice cream and Toraichi towel.

While the store caters to port workers, you don’t have to be a port worker to make a purchase, so Mr Sato highly recommends stopping by if you ever see one during your travels. It’s a unique take on the Japanese convenience store and a nice reminder of how big-name chains can adapt their brand to serve the needs of the local community.

Store information
Port Store Aomi / Port Store青海
Address: Tokyo-to Koto-ku Aomi 4-4-1
東京都江東区青海4-4-1
Open 24 hours

title: Lawson convenience store opens its first mobile, trailer-style location in Japan
description: The new mobile model is also being considered for use in disaster-stricken areas. The future of Japanese convenience stores may be on wheels. Located at the south side of the gymnasium at Ebina Sports Park in Kanagawa Prefecture, a new type of trailer-style Lawson convenience store opened for business on August 27. It’s slated to […]
content:
The new mobile model is also being considered for use in disaster-stricken areas.

The future of Japanese convenience stores may be on wheels.

Located at the south side of the gymnasium at Ebina Sports Park in Kanagawa Prefecture, a new type of trailer-style Lawson convenience store opened for business on August 27. It’s slated to be in operation through March 31 as the chain tests its viability to make an impact on the market. Not having a fixed physical building lowers the cost and allows the chain to make inroads in places that were previously inaccessible and lacking konbini, as Japanese convenience stores are fondly nicknamed. Plus, as it’s portable and relatively easy to set up, officials are taking into account its serious potential to be at the forefront of relief efforts for when disasters such as earthquakes strike across the country.

▼ The new trailer-style Lawson konbini

The interior is about one-fifth the size of an ordinary Lawson store with a total length of 12.2 meters (40 feet).  It carries around 500 items for sale including prepared foods such as bento, onigiri, fried foods, and desserts, as well as drinks and other daily necessities. A 6.1-meter (20-foot) long kitchen/office space is also attached where the foods are prepared. However, some things have to go given the limited space, so this branch is missing the usual ATM, copy machine, and Loppi ticket kiosk found at regular Lawson store locations.

▼ The total area of the store space is a snug 33.60 square meters (361.7 square feet).

Time will tell if this new type of Lawson proves viable in the long run among the already oversaturated konbini market with new contenders popping up every so often. However, given the weight of Lawson’s name as one of the “Big 3” konbini and the uniquely positioned ability of this mobile model to be accessible in times of need, we’ll tentatively say that it looks like the future’s on wheels.

title: Japan Railways announces unlimited-ride train pass for fall travel
description: A great way to explores off-the-beaten-path Japan this autumn. You can make a strong argument that fall is the best time of year to travel in Japan. In summer you’ve got heat, humidity, rainstorms, and large crowds of both domestic and international tourists to contend with. In spring, you might also run into crowds and […]
content:
A great way to explores off-the-beaten-path Japan this autumn.

You can make a strong argument that fall is the best time of year to travel in Japan. In summer you’ve got heat, humidity, rainstorms, and large crowds of both domestic and international tourists to contend with. In spring, you might also run into crowds and inflated hotel prices because of the cherry blossoms, and, while winter tends to be the least crowded season, that’s largely because many parts of Japan aren’t much fun to be in when it’s cold and snowy.

Autumn, though, comes with hardly any of those downsides, and now it’s looking like an even better season in which to explore the country thanks to the announcement by JR/Japan Railways Group of its new Unlimited Autumn Ride rail pass.

Called the Aki no Norihodai Pass in Japanese, this deal gives you three full days of unlimited rides on JR regular and rapid (kaisoku) trains. There aren’t any regional restrictions, either – the pass lets you ride regular and kaisoku trains on any JR line in Japan.

There is a catch, in that the pass doesn’t get you onto express and special express trains, so it can’t be used on the Shinkansen. With many of Japan’s standard-itinerary sightseeing attractions along the major bullet train routes dealing with overtourism these days, however, there’s a lot of value in taking the time to explore off-the-beaten-path parts of country via its more local lines, and the Unlimited Autumn Ride pass also gives you unlimited rides on JR-managed BRT highway buses.

The pass is priced at 7,850 yen (US$49) for adults and 3,920 yen for children, so it shouldn’t be hard to get your money’s worth out of it on an extended-weekend trip. For travelers headed up to Japan’s northernmost prefecture, Hokkaido, there’s also a Hokkaido Shinkansen Option ticket (4,650 yen for adults, 2,320 yen for kids) that can be used in tandem with the pass and allows for a one-time ride between Shin Aomori and Kikonai Stations on the Hokkaido Shinkansen line and one ride on the non-JR Donan Isaribi Tetsudo Line from Kikonai to Goryokaku Station, from which JR lines can be accessed.

The passes will be on sale from September 18 to October 16 at major JR stations, JR travel centers, and third-party travel agencies and can be used for a period of three consecutive days between October 3 and 18.

title: Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon Ice Cream makes us rethink everything we thought we knew about sweets
description: This noodle dessert makes our brains malfunction. When it comes to Kagawa, udon is king. content:
This noodle dessert makes our brains malfunction.

When it comes to Kagawa, udon is king. Not only is the climate ideal for growing wheat – udon is a wheat noodle – but locals in Kagawa eat more udon per person than anywhere else in Japan, leading it to be dubbed Japan’s “Udon Prefecture”, a moniker that Kagawa proudly stands by.

We were reminded of just how strong the links are between noodles and the prefecture when, on a recent trip to the area, we spotted a sign outside a beautiful old shop along the approach to Kompirasan, one of the region’s most famous shrines.

▼ The sign, posted at the Konpira Udon Sando Store, read: “Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon-style Soft Serve”.


Having travelled to different parts of Japan, we knew that turning local specialties into ice cream has become something of a thing in recent years, but we were surprised to see udon being used this way. Making it even more unusual was the fact that the ice cream was based on onsen egg bukkake udon, one of our favourite noodle dishes. As fans of the dish, we were curious to find out how well the ice cream could replicate its look and flavour, so we decided to step into the shop and order a real onsen egg bukkake udon and the soft serve to see how they would compare.

▼ Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon at 730 yen (US$4.90) on the left, Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon-style Soft Serve (580 yen) on the right.

It only took about five minutes for both dishes to arrive, and when they did, we were charmed by how the shape and size of the bowls were almost identical.

▼ What wasn’t identical, though, was what was inside them.

There, on the right, was a bowl of white goodness that had a noodly look to it, and on top, a slice of lemon and the onsen egg, two ingredients you would usually find in a bowl of Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon.

▼ Look closely and you’ll see a splash (“bukkake” means “splash”) of sauce resembling soy sauce-based dashi within the “noodles”.

The presentation was so convincing in person that we momentarily forgot this was ice cream until we saw the dessert spoon there in place of chopsticks. Resisting the urge to gobble it down right away, we stopped to try the actual noodles on the left hand side of the tray.

▼ Absolutely delicious.

Kagawa udon truly is something else – the noodles had a wonderfully firm and slippery texture, and the balance of the dashi was perfect. After gently breaking the onsen egg apart and mixing it through the noodles, the flavour became smoother and richer, with the oil from the tempura crumbs and aroma of green onions adding just the right amount of texture and freshness to the dish.

▼ Time to try the Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon-style Soft Serve.

Releasing the yolk on this dish felt entirely wrong because, well…when would you normally break an egg over ice cream? Still, this is exactly how the dish is meant to be eaten, so we watched as the orange yolk slowly flowed over the white cream, creating an unorthodox, and sinful-looking, dessert.

▼ Gently mixing some of the yolk into the ice cream, we lifted a spoonful up for a taste, and…

▼ …what the heck is this?

The richness and saltiness of the yolk subdued the sweetness of the cream, shifting the flavour from something that felt like a dessert towards something more like a meal. We never imagined that egg yolk and ice cream would work so well together, but when we stopped to think about it, we realised that both custard and ice cream contain egg yolk, so perhaps the pairing makes perfect sense. Still, there was something entirely different about eating ice cream with a runny onsen egg oozing over it, and though it was odd, it wasn’t bad at all.

Curious to find out how lemon would affect the flavours, we first squirted some on the real noodle dish to get a sense of the taste.

▼ Yep, a classic combination that’s totally delicious.

We then  squeezed the lemon over our onsen egg ice cream, and…

▼… this worked surprisingly well too!

As soon as the acidity came into play, the finish became much lighter, lifting the sweet and salty richness of the dessert with a delicious freshness. It was genuinely a new and interesting kind of dessert, and so good that we could see ourselves becoming seriously addicted to it.

The flavour was so captivating that we interspersed the experience with mouthfuls of udon, which really broke our brain.

▼ Udon!

▼ Soft serve!


▼ Udon!!

▼ Soft serve!!!

Eventually, our taste buds started to become very confused, and at that point our brain malfunctioned and we wound up doing the unthinkable: we mixed the udon and ice cream together. This turned out be another surprise, as the two dishes worked together far better than expected, and we easily polished off the whole thing.

By the end of our very unorthodox meal, we realised two things. First, the Onsen Egg Bukkake Udon-style Soft Serve is an udon-inspired dessert that does a very good job of looking like a noodle dish. Secondly, we’ve rarely ever eaten a dessert with this level of attention to detail before.

From making it look like udon, which is no easy feat when you’re working with a soft ingredient, right through to the bowl and presentation, and the idea to include the onsen egg and lemon, which transforms the flavour while you eat, every element has clearly been carefully designed for the diner’s enjoyment.

Even when eaten alongside our beloved onsen egg bukkake udon, the soft serve held its own as a dessert, and we highly recommend trying it if you can. It’ll become a dessert to remember, and a nice way to reward yourself after climbing the shrine’s 785 stairs.

Restaurant information

Konpira Udon Sando Store / こんぴらうどん参道店
Address: Kagawa-ken Nakatado-gun Kotohira-cho 810-3
香川県仲多度郡琴平町810-3
Open: 8 a.m.–5 p.m.
